title: Thinking and Participation Ratios: Maximising Cognitive Engagement
author: Busch, Bradley
summary: In an interview format, InnerDrive's Bradley Busch and Doug Lemov unpack the concepts of "participation ratio," what percentage of the class is actively participating, and "think ratio," how hard and deep students are thinking, which Lemov reframes through a cognitive-science lens as whether thinking is sufficient to cause encoding and memory formation. Lemov details specific techniques for raising participation ratio: cold-calling, turn and talk, wait time, and stop-and-jot, framing cold-calling specifically as a message that "your voice matters" rather than a punitive tool. He names and explains two failure modes: "crickets," where silence pushes teachers toward easier questions rather than toward cold-calling or turn-and-talk, and the same handful of highly verbal students dominating discussion, which lowers both participation and think ratio because rapid, impulsive answers are shallow. He introduces "shallow land," where high participation masks low cognitive challenge, while conceding it has a legitimate limited use as a confidence-building warm-up before ratcheting up rigor. The piece closes with Lemov's case for planning both questions and exemplar answers in advance, arguing this frees working memory during the lesson to actually listen to what students say, and InnerDrive links two recent cognitive-science studies that independently support the value of harder retrieval questions and classroom talk.
points: Lemov's redefinition of "think ratio" through cognitive science, asking whether there is deliberate difficulty sufficient to cause encoding, sharpens the concept beyond his earlier "rigor of the question" framing.

His diagnosis of "crickets" identifies a specific teacher failure mode: awkward silence pushes teachers toward easier questions rather than toward tools like cold call or turn and talk that would actually solve the participation problem.
"Shallow land" names a subtle trap: high participation ratio can create a false sense that a lesson is working, when the questions driving it are too easy to build real understanding.

Lemov's case for "exemplar planning," writing out the ideal answer to key questions in advance, is framed around a specific cognitive mechanism: it frees the teacher's working memory to actually listen to students' answers in the moment.
quotes: Participation ratio is the percentage of the class who are actively participating in the lesson, while think ratio is how hard and deep students are thinking.
Cold-Calling – This is calling on a student regardless of whether they have offered to participate. This allows you to invite everyone—even hesitant students into the discussion.

The first is “crickets”, where the teacher asks the questions and students just look at you with no answer. Because this is awkward, teachers often ask simpler questions afterwards as they think no one wants to participate.

Shallow land” is an area which looks like learning; but in reality, it’s all happening at the surface level. This is normally derived from easy and poorly designed questions that lead to low cognitive challenges.
This study found that although students may prefer easy questions when it comes to retrieval, they actually learned more from the more challenging ones.
